claims.text: The starting protective coating is an FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy with a baseline interphase spacing and microstructural scale.
Increasing the cooling rate during deposition will refine the coating microstructure.
Increasing the cooling rate during deposition will increase the density of coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries relative to the control coating.
The standard coating has a lower interphase-boundary density than the coating produced with faster cooling.
Coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Refined interphase boundaries impede dislocation glide during sustained loading.
Refined interphase boundaries impede dislocation climb during sustained loading.
Interphase boundaries pin dislocations and thereby reduce the creep strain rate.
Increasing coherent FCC/BCC interphase-boundary density will enhance creep resistance under sustained loading.
Compared under identical sustained-stress conditions, the faster-cooled coating will exhibit less creep strain than the baseline coating.
Compared under identical sustained-stress conditions, the faster-cooled coating will exhibit a lower creep rate than the baseline coating.
The proposed mechanism is expected to govern under constant sub-yield stress at a service-relevant temperature.
Outside the specified sustained-stress and temperature boundaries, other deformation mechanisms may dominate.
Failure of the faster-cooled coating to show a statistically significant reduction in creep strain or creep rate relative to the control would falsify the proposed hypothesis.
